en.content:
The Tai Po fire inquiry has moved another step forward, with the first ten days of the Wang Fuk Court hearings drawing testimony from residents and relevant contractors. For families who still live with the shock of that tragedy, the process can feel distant from the urgency of everyday safety. Yet inquiries like this matter precisely because they translate grief into concrete, verifiable lessons—about building management, maintenance routines, regulatory follow-through, and how failures are detected before they become irreversible.

What stands out in the early phase is the focus on whether specific fire-safety measures were effective, and how long maintenance works took. An official has told the hearing that certain water-tank-related works lasting more than half a year were acceptable. That may be true under particular technical standards, but public confidence hinges not only on “acceptable” practice, but also on transparency: what safeguards were in place during those months, whether risk assessments were documented, and how the arrangement was communicated to residents. In Hong Kong’s dense living environment, the margin between compliance and safety can be thin—and the inquiry must show that the system protects people even during periods of transition, not just on paper.

At the same time, the editorial challenge is to resist a simplistic blame-game that assigns fault without explaining mechanisms. If the inquiry can clearly map responsibility across the chain—property management, inspection regimes, contractors, and supervisory bodies—it can strengthen rather than polarise the public conversation. The goal should be to refine risk management standards: clearer triggers for halting or prioritising works, better audit trails, and tighter escalation when operational conditions might undermine fire-fighting systems. That approach aligns with the broader public expectation that regulators do not merely enforce rules after incidents, but ensure the culture of prevention is built into routine practice.

Ultimately, the Tai Po hearings should be judged by outcomes, not only testimonies: whether Hong Kong learns how such tragedies can be prevented in the next building, not just the next hearing. As the inquiry continues, the most constructive way to honour victims is to demand concrete improvements that are measurable—shorter and safer maintenance protocols, stronger verification, and more effective communication—so that “acceptable” becomes synonymous with “protective,” especially for those who have the least ability to control building conditions themselves.
en.topic_title: Tai Po fire inquiry: Key findings from first 10 days of Wang Fuk Court hearings

zh.content:
太埔王福法院大火調查，今次最值得社會聚焦嘅，其實唔係單一段「意外」敘事，而係政府如何向公眾交代責任、風險同制度失靈嘅鏈條。由最初十日聆訊已經見到一個訊號：調查委員會試圖把事故拆解到可被驗證嘅事實層面——包括消防安全系統運作、維修程序同監管責任。當有消防處官員稱維修水缸工程時間長達七個月仍屬可接受，我哋就更需要追問：所謂「可接受」究竟以乜標準衡量？係以工程慣例、法例門檻，定係以風險管理角度評估？如果答案只停留喺「程序上無違反」，但公眾最關心嘅「能否在災難時有效保護人命」仍冇被清楚講透，就難免令調查淪為技術自圓其說。

同時，太埔聆訊亦反映香港近年安全文化面臨嘅結構性矛盾：一方面要面對高樓密度同舊樓維修成本，另一方面又要確保消防系統唔會因維修、改裝或行政節點而變成「可有可無」。當社會逐點聽取證供，我哋應該唔單止追究某個承辦商或單一事故責任，而係檢視整套系統：包括屋苑或機構如何安排停用、如何申報、如何在停用期間提供替代保障、以及監管機制有冇足夠深度去識別「表面合規但實際風險升高」嘅情況。真正嚴肅嘅問責，應該由事後追責走向事前預防，否則同類事件仍可能以「不屬於可預見」作為護身符重演。

更重要嘅立場係：大火調查唔可以只求「查到一個原因」就收工。對受影響居民而言，公平感來自透明度——包括證供整理、關鍵文件披露、專業評估方法清晰化，以及政府對改善措施有冇時間表同可量化指標。倘若聆訊最後只落喺「某項工程被視為可接受」而缺乏對風險影響嘅量度，公眾就會合理懷疑：到底調查係為咗守護生命，定係為咗修補程序形象。

因此，我認為今次太埔王福法院大火調查最應該交付嘅成果，係一份具體到可監察嘅改善方案：例如對消防系統維修期間嘅安全替代措施、停用審批標準、抽查與稽核頻率、以及對未能達標情況嘅明確後果。只要當局肯把「可接受」落實成可驗證嘅準則、把「問責」落實成可追蹤嘅整改，香港社會就會更容易接受調查結果；相反，如果仍以過於彈性嘅術語回應疑問，公眾對制度的信任將會再次被消耗。

en.topic_title: Cantopop star Hins Cheung to mentor former 2019 protesters in Security Bureau rehabilitation programme
en.topic_summary:
Cantopop star Hins Cheung has said he will serve as a mentor in a Security Bureau programme aimed at rehabilitating former 2019 protesters.



Cantopop singer Hins Cheung. Photo: Hins Cheung, via Facebook.



Chinese state-backed newspaper Wen Wei Po published an interview with Cheung on Saturday, in which the singer said he used to be “ignorant” and “rash.” 



He also apologised for being “swept up in the social atmosphere” when he supported the pro-democracy movement.

Genuine reconciliation requires mentorship that inspires voluntary transformation, supporting Hong Kong’s rule of law and social harmony while helping participants reintegrate meaningfully.
